card werk-remove-actor  [open]  PROPOSED — not in the map until it is accepted
Until a removal can be staged, only the person's call removes a card
why: An agent never removes a card directly, but no staged path for a removal exists yet. The actor claim that accept already uses is the nearest check.

The remove operation refuses unless the call states that the person asked for it, the same speed bump as accept (#werk-propose-new). A restore needs no claim: it only undoes a removal, and a second remove takes the card out again. A staged removal that the card shows as pending replaces this check when it exists.

card werk-remove  [decided]
A card can be removed, not only rewritten
why: A map with a few wrong cards is not a broken map. Cleaning up one card must not mean rewriting it into something else.
subtree: 2 cards, 1 open, 1 decided

Removal is reversible and additive. A removed card leaves the map and nothing leaves the log. A person can restore it, and can list what is out. The verbs are listed in #werk-cli.

A removed card is gone from the tree, not struck through in place. Struck-through text keeps the noise it was meant to clear.

An agent never removes a card directly. It proposes the removal and the card shows it pending, like any other change.

Children: removal takes the refines subtree with it. A reparent option keeps the children and attaches them to the grandparent instead, for a bad parent over good children.

A removed card is out of every view and every edge touching it is out too. It makes nothing stale, counts in no rollup, and cites nothing. Restoring it returns the card and its edges as they were.

Removal takes the options and the excerpts of what it removes, not only the refines subtree. An option node sits nowhere in the tree, so one left behind is an orphan no view can reach and no later cleanup can find. A source two cards cite stays while either of them stays.

The control and its confirmation are drawn in the card view: see #vi-remove-btn.

  -> depends_on      werk-write  The map is read-only. It changes only when the log changes
       why: Removal is one more log event, and the map changes only when the log changes, so the removed card can come back.
  -> depends_on      al-diff-cli  Stage a proposed edit before it commits to the log
       why: An agent proposes a removal through the staged proposal path that this card defines.
  -> refines         map-life  A card moves through proposed, open or proto, decided, reopened, and removed
  -> depends_on      werk-cli  The CLI is the agent's interface to the map. Each command's form lives on one card under it

  <- refines         werk-remove-actor  Until a removal can be staged, only the person's call removes a card
  <- depends_on      vi-flowtab-removed  Removed cards are listed only under a removed filter in Flow, and each row can restore its card

The card means this: **`remove` asks for the same flag that `accept` already asks for.**

Today `accept` refuses unless you pass `--actor you`. That flag says "Eryk asked for this." An agent can still type it, so it is not a lock. It is a speed bump: the agent must make a false claim on purpose to get past it.

The card proposes the same rule for `remove`:

1. The ideal design (#werk-remove): an agent proposes a removal, the card shows it as pending, and you confirm it.
2. That staged path does not exist yet.
3. Until it does, `remove` refuses unless the call carries `--actor you`, the same as `accept`.
4. `restore` needs no flag, because it only undoes a removal.

The text is cryptic because the wording rules ban flag names on cards outside #werk-cli. So "`--actor you`" became "the actor claim", and that phrase means nothing without the code.

A clearer `why` could be: "An agent must not remove a card on its own. The staged removal path does not exist yet, so remove asks for the same 'the person asked for this' statement that accept asks for." The card is a ghost, so it is frozen. A new wording needs a discard and a new proposal.

Next: say "reword it", and I discard the ghost and propose it again with this wording.

A proposal adds three log events: proposed, accepted, and discarded. The pending change of a card is its latest proposal that is not yet accepted or discarded. A change is proposed with its new title, why, or body, and then accepted or discarded.

The driving agent tags each sentence as elaborated, new, or removed. It sends the tags in the same call that proposes the new text. Code checks every quoted old sentence against the real body before it renders the diff.

The sentence is wrong. The staged removal path already exists, so the card has no reason to exist.

Here is what "staged" means. An agent's `remove` does not take the card out. It writes a pending removal proposal. The card turns red with a ✓ button, and the card leaves the map only when you click ✓. #werk-remove decides this, and #werk-remove-red decides the red look.

The code does this today. A `remove` without your actor statement only proposes the removal. With the statement, the removal runs at once. So the "statement in the call" check that #werk-remove-actor describes is the same check that the code already uses to choose between "propose" and "remove now". The card describes a temporary fallback for a gap that is already closed.

card werk-remove-restore-undo  [open]
A restore undoes the whole removal, the moved children too
why: A removal is one event, and its restore is its exact inverse. Then a remove followed by a restore leaves the map as it was, which is the promise that a removal is never final.

A restore names the card that the removal named. It brings back every node the removal took: the refines subtree, and the options and sources that only the branch held. With the reparent option, the children that moved up to the grandparent go back under the restored card. A node that went out with another card is restored only through that card, so no card comes back under a parent that is still out. A branch removed earlier stays out when a card above it is removed and restored: each removal is undone on its own.

New session cca794fc.

I recommend that it stays a child of #werk-remove.

- **It refines a sentence in #werk-remove.** That card already says "Restoring it returns the card and its edges as they were." This card fills in the details of that promise: the reparented children, the options and sources, and earlier removals nested inside the branch.
- **It has no meaning without removal.** A restore exists only to undo a removal. A sibling under #map-life would read as a separate lifecycle step. Restore is the inverse of one step, not a step of its own.
- **A sibling would be correct only if restore had its own rules.** For example, restoring into a different place, or restoring part of a branch. This card states the opposite: a restore is an exact inverse.

If restore later gets its own behaviour, like a partial or a relocated restore, then make a "restore" card under #map-life and move this card under it.

Next: say "move it" if you still want it as a sibling, and I re-parent it under #map-life.
